What the function does. `handoffCausalCapabilities` takes the caller-supplied Graph, FullCausalCapability, expected CausalBinding and recipient callback. It first calls `assertCausalCapabilities(graph, capabilities, expected)` (packages/ts/src/solutions/causal-occurrence/capabilities.ts:67-90). That function looks the value up in the module-private `issued` WeakMap (capabilities.ts:51) and throws `TypeError("causal capability binding mismatch")` when the value is absent (a structural copy or cast), when `root.graph !== graph` (a different Graph), when `root.level !== "full"`, or when contract/implementationRevision/scope/epoch differ from the expected binding (capabilities.ts:72-82). It then walks `full.identity`, `full.execution`, `full.retained`, requiring each to be an issued record with the same `instance` and `graph` (capabilities.ts:83-87), and finally requires `full.execution.identity === full.identity` and `full.retained.execution === full.execution` (capabilities.ts:88-89). Because the throw happens before `recipient(levels)`, the recipient is not called for a structural copy, a foreign-Graph capability or a binding mismatch. The README states the same rule: "A capability validation failure must be handled before passing the capabilities to a recipient; a structural copy is not an issued object" (examples/spending-alerts/README.md:41-43).

Identity preservation. The three levels are forwarded as the original references (`capabilities.identity`, `capabilities.execution`, `capabilities.retained`), not rebuilt. `createCausalCapabilities` freezes the nested objects so that `execution.identity` is the very same `identity` object and `retained.execution` is the very same `execution` object (capabilities.ts:122-138), and the demo asserts exactly these equalities: `assert.equal(execution, app.capabilities.execution)`, `assert.equal(execution.identity, app.capabilities.identity)`, `assert.equal(app.capabilities.retained.execution, execution)` (examples/spending-alerts/causal-graded-demo.ts:85-87). The framework example likewise returns `capabilities.execution` unchanged after validation (examples/spending-alerts/causal-audience.examples.ts:18-25). The wrapper object I build is a fresh frozen record of those same references; it does not copy or re-issue the capability objects, so the WeakMap identity and the lower-handle lineage remain intact.

Does possession of the execution level authorize an arbitrary I/O call? No. The execution level is a passive set of Node handles: `ExecutionCapability` exposes `identity`, `terminals`, `conservation` and `causalQuiescence` (capabilities.ts:27-32), and `FullCausalCapability` adds only `retained` and `startup` (capabilities.ts:38-43). There is no write/open/execute method anywhere in these interfaces. The README says "Capabilities have no arbitrary I/O execution method" (README.md:91) and the audience example comments "an execution view grants no I/O method" (causal-audience.examples.ts:17). Actual I/O is gated elsewhere and separately: the host guard requires an admitted effect, a passing independent verification receipt, a non-revoked local grant whose `admissionRef` equals the hash of proposal+receipt+grant+binding, a current watermark, and a ready inbox with one free slot (causal-focused-host.ts:404-431); only then does it call `lease.write(payload)` (causal-focused-host.ts:455), and the lease itself refuses writes unless it was transferred (causal-resource.ts:76-98). The README also notes that a publication saying "succeeded" is only that exact request's simulated result, and that startup/readiness facts do not prove authorization or completion (README.md:99-105). So the execution level conveys observation of lifecycle/terminal/conservation facts, not authority to perform arbitrary I/O.
